vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: intelligence-suite
Version: 1.0.1

The OpenClaw skill bundle 'intelligence-suite' is designed for AI and global news monitoring. The `scripts/monitor.js` and `scripts/scan.js` files use standard Node.js libraries (`axios`, `cheerio`, `rss-parser`) to fetch and parse content from legitimate news sources and APIs (e.g., Reuters, SCMP, OpenAI, Hacker News). All network activity is directly related to the stated purpose, and there is no evidence of data exfiltration, malicious execution, persistence, or prompt injection attempts in `SKILL.md` beyond standard usage instructions. The code is clear, readable, and lacks any obfuscation or suspicious dependencies.

llm.summary: The skill's description (news/monitoring) matches the included scripts, but there are inconsistencies and missing controls: bundled Node.js code will be executed with no install guidance, no declared dependencies or envs, and the model can invoke it — this could run arbitrary network/file operations without the user knowing.

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose (AI and global news monitoring) aligns with having scripts named scan.js and monitor.js. However SKILL.md metadata requires the 'node' binary while the registry metadata reported 'required binaries: none' — that's an inconsistency. package.json and JS scripts are present (so Node is realistically required).
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions tell the agent to run bundled scripts (node scripts/scan.js --report, node scripts/monitor.js --report). Those scripts can perform arbitrary network and filesystem operations; SKILL.md does not document what endpoints are contacted, what data is collected, or any limits on behavior. Because execution is delegated to bundled code, the instructions allow broad, underspecified actions outside the high-level description.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec even though package.json exists. That means no explicit npm install step is declared; it's unclear whether dependencies are vendored or required. If an agent or user runs npm install later, external packages could be pulled without prior review. The lack of an install mechanism combined with executable scripts is a red flag.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables or credentials, which superficially matches a public news-monitoring tool. However, the bundled scripts could still read environment variables or local files at runtime (not declared in requires.env). The absence of declared secrets is appropriate, but it doesn't prevent the code from accessing secrets if executed.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not marked 'always:true' but disableModelInvocation is not set — the model may invoke this skill autonomously. Combined with bundled executable code that can make network calls and access the filesystem, that makes autonomous invocation potentially risky unless you trust the code. No additional privilege-limiting metadata is present.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This package contains executable JavaScript (monitor.js and scan.js) but provides no install steps or visibility into what the scripts do. Before installing or enabling the skill: 1) Inspect the contents of scripts/scan.js, scripts/monitor.js and package.json to see what network endpoints are contacted, whether any env vars or local files are read, and which npm dependencies are required. 2) If you can't review the code, run it only in a sandboxed/isolated environment (container or VM) with no secrets mounted and restricted network access. 3) If you plan to enable model-driven invocation, consider disabling autonomous invocation until you've reviewed the code. 4) If npm dependencies are required, verify they come from reputable packages and run a dependency audit. 5) Ask the publisher for a homepage/source URL and a clear explanation of what data the skill collects and transmits; absence of that information is a practical risk. Proceed only after these checks.
